titel: The share as a stake in a company
kurz: What you own legally and economically when you hold a share, and why the share price only shows the price on the day in question.

bloecke.md:
A share is a stake in the [[Share capital|share capital]] of a public limited company (Aktiengesellschaft, AG). The Stock Corporation Act (Aktiengesetz, AktG) sets out the key points in a few provisions. The share capital amounts to at least €50,000 (Section 7 AktG). At least one euro of it must be attributable to each [[No-par-value share|no-par-value share]] (Section 8 AktG), and the share is indivisible. Only the company's assets are liable for the company's debts (Section 1 AktG). A shareholder can therefore lose at most the money they have invested.

Economically, a share represents more than a price. It is a claim to a fraction of everything a company owns and will earn in the future. What it owns includes, for example, its plant, its brand, its patents, its customer contracts and its cash reserves. The shareholder's claim relates to what is left after all other claims have been met.

bloecke.titel: Rights attached to a German share

One share, one vote; exceptions only through preference shares or multiple-voting shares
Admission to the annual general meeting and information on the company's affairs
In a capital increase you can maintain your percentage holding instead of being diluted
Only what remains after all liabilities have been settled
No recourse to the shareholder's private assets

bloecke.md: The penultimate row of the table is the most important. The shareholder has a [[Residual claim|residual claim]] and is served last. Wages, suppliers, interest and taxes are paid first, and only what remains after that belongs to the owners. This explains both the historically higher return on shares and their fluctuations. Because the owners are served last, they receive a disproportionately large amount in good years and nothing in bad years. A bond issued by the same company, by contrast, represents a fixed, senior claim and therefore has a completely different return and risk profile.

bloecke.titel: Business and stock exchange trading as separate cycles
bloecke.unter: No arrow leads from the stock exchange back into the company, because trading only transfers ownership between investors and does not directly affect the operating business.

knoten.notiz: the remainder that belongs to the owners

bloecke.md:
An investor who buys €10,000 worth of shares on the stock exchange today gives the company none of it. The money goes to the seller, that is, to another investor. Fresh capital flows to the company only at the initial issue and in a capital increase. The stock exchange is the secondary market on which shares that have already been issued change owners.

That is why a falling share price does not initially affect the operating business. The company has not lost any money, and the machines keep running. The share price only feeds back into the company indirectly, namely through the terms of a capital increase, the interest of potential acquirers, share-based payment and the way lenders perceive the company.

A company has 500 million shares outstanding and earns €2 billion a year after tax. That makes €4.00 of annual profit per share.

An investor with 100 shares owns one five-millionth of the company and therefore, arithmetically, €400 of this annual profit. This applies regardless of whether part of it is distributed or everything stays in the company. Distributed profits land in the shareholder's account; retained profits continue to belong to the shareholder proportionately as part of the company.

If the share costs €60 on the stock exchange, the market values the entire equity at €30 billion. This amount is called [[Market capitalisation|market capitalisation]]. A buyer then pays €15 for every euro of annual profit. If the price falls to €40, the figures are €20 billion and €10 per euro of profit. Nothing about the company has changed, only the price that other investors are asking for it.

## Price and business

Warren Buffett explained the separation of price and business with an example that does not involve a stock exchange. In 1986 he bought a 400-acre farm in Nebraska for $280,000. That was about $700 per acre and considerably less than a failed bank had lent against the farm a few years earlier. Buffett knew nothing about farming. But one of his sons worked out for him how much corn and soybeans the land would produce and what it would cost to farm it. This gave an expected return of about 10% on the purchase price.

By the 2013 annual report, which Buffett wrote in February 2014, the farm's earnings had tripled and its value had risen at least fivefold. Over those 28 years, that corresponds to about 5.9% appreciation a year, in addition to the ongoing income. Buffett visited the farm twice in that time and never saw a quoted price for it. By his reasoning, a moody neighbour shouting a price for the farm at him every day would not have changed the corn yields either. With shares, there is such a neighbour, because the stock exchange quotes a price on every trading day.

Benjamin Graham introduced the figure in 1949 in *The Intelligent Investor*. In the fourth edition of 1973 it appears in the eighth chapter. He describes a co-owner of a business whose partner names a price every day. At that price, the partner offers either to buy the co-owner's stake or to sell him his own. Sometimes the price makes sense; often it is driven by euphoria or panic. The partner does not force the co-owner into anything and names a new price the next day.

Warren Buffett adopted the figure in Berkshire's 1987 annual report and added, in essence, that anyone who cannot value their business far better than [[Mr Market]] does not belong in the game. The figure is useful because it reverses the perspective. Investors judge the price against their own assessment instead of taking the price as a verdict on their decision.

Price and value therefore have to be distinguished. The **price** is the most recent price on which two market participants agreed. The **value** is what the company can pay out to its owners over its lifetime, discounted to today. The price is observable, accurate to two decimal places and available at any time. That is why it is easily confused with the value, which is what the investor is concerned with. Value cannot be observed. It can only be estimated, and the estimate has a wide range.

The divergence between price and value can be measured by smoothing the denominator of a valuation ratio. The cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio relates the price to the inflation-adjusted ten-year average of earnings. As a result, the denominator changes only slowly, yet the ratio still fluctuates strongly.

bloecke.unter: Shiller CAPE, that is, price divided by the inflation-adjusted ten-year average of earnings. Although the denominator is deliberately smoothed, the annual values (each for January) ranged between 5.12 (1921) and 43.77 (2000), and the monthly values between 4.78 (December 1920) and 44.19 (December 1999). The mean since 1871 is 17.4, and the level on 13 October 2026 is 41.84.

bloecke.md:
## Ownership and control

Two German peculiarities shift the relationship between share of capital and influence. The first is the non-voting [[Preference share|preference share]]. It may account for at most half of the share capital (Section 139 AktG), and in return for giving up the voting right its holders receive a preferential or additional dividend. Henkel AG & Co. KGaA, for example, has issued both classes: around 260 million ordinary shares and around 178 million preference shares. It is the preference share that is included in the DAX, while just over 61% of the ordinary shares are held by the family under a shareholder pooling agreement. Under these circumstances, the voting right attached to the ordinary share has no practical effect for a small investor. The price gap between the two classes therefore reflects less the value of the vote than differences in tradability and index demand. It is not constant, and depending on the point in time, either the preference share or the ordinary share can be more expensive.

The second peculiarity is new. Since the Future Financing Act (Zukunftsfinanzierungsgesetz), multiple voting rights have been permitted again. Section 135a AktG allows registered shares with up to ten votes per share. For listed companies, the multiple voting rights lapse when the share is transferred and at the latest ten years after the IPO. The articles of association can extend this period once by up to ten years. This requires a majority of three-quarters of the share capital represented when the resolution is adopted. Buying shares therefore does not automatically bring a proportionate share of control. In addition, with the KGaA legal form (partnership limited by shares), management lies with the general partner, and the annual general meeting can accordingly achieve less.

The first fallacy is: *The price has fallen, so the company has got worse.* But prices also fall because a major shareholder needs liquidity, because an index is reconstituted, because interest rates rise or because an entire sector has gone out of fashion. None of these reasons concerns the operating business.

The second fallacy is the mirror image of the first: *The price has fallen, so the share is cheap.* Sometimes the price falls because the business is collapsing, and then it is still too high even after the decline. Both statements derive a conclusion about value directly from a price movement. Whether a price is favourable can only be judged with your own idea of the value.

The price shows what other investors are paying for a share today. The value depends on what the business will earn in the future. The two move independently of each other, and only the price can be seen on the screen.

German shares exist as bearer shares (Inhaberaktien) and as registered shares (Namensaktien). With a registered share, the owner is entered in the company's share register (Section 67 AktG). The company therefore knows its shareholders and can contact them directly. With a bearer share, proof of entitlement is provided via the custodian bank. Multiple voting rights under Section 135a AktG require registered shares. A company that wants to issue such shares must therefore first switch to registered shares.

Physical share certificates, that is, printed documents, play practically no role any more. The issue is held as a global certificate by the central securities depository (Wertpapiersammelbank), and the securities account shows a co-ownership share in it. This does not change the rights under Sections 58, 118 or 186 AktG.

Before your next purchase, write down two sentences: first, what the company sells, to whom and where its profit comes from; second, what price you are paying and what annual profit you get for it.

If you cannot write the first sentence, you do not know which business you are taking a stake in with the share. If you can, you have a yardstick against which a falling price can be measured. You are then not dependent on Mr Market to judge whether the decision was right.

mitnehmen: A share is an indivisible fraction of the share capital and therefore a claim to the remainder that is left after wages, suppliers, interest and taxes.
Purchases on the stock exchange bring the company no money. Fresh capital flows to it only at issue and in capital increases.

Since 1900, the price of one dollar of smoothed corporate earnings on the US stock market ranged between 5.12 and 43.77 in the annual values, while the smoothed earnings themselves fluctuated far less.
Mr Market makes an offer every day that you do not have to accept. You can only make use of the offer if you have your own idea of the value.
In Germany, share of capital and control can be separated through preference shares and, since Section 135a AktG, also through multiple voting rights. This should be checked before buying.

begriffe.text: The nominal capital of an AG (public limited company) laid down in its articles of association, at least €50,000 (Section 7 AktG). It is divided into shares and determines what fraction of the company a single share represents.

A share without a nominal amount. Its portion of the share capital results solely from the number of shares. At least one euro of share capital must be attributable to each no-par-value share (Section 8 AktG), and shares are indivisible.
A class of shares without voting rights whose holders receive a preferential or additional dividend in return. It may account for at most half of the share capital (Section 139 AktG).
A claim to what is left after all senior claims have been met. It distinguishes equity from debt and is the reason for its higher expected return and greater fluctuation.
Share price times the number of shares outstanding. It states the price the market currently puts on a company's entire equity and is not a balance sheet item.

A figure devised by Benjamin Graham. Mr Market is a business partner who names a price for your stake every day, sometimes reasonable, sometimes driven by fear or greed. You may accept his offer, respond to it or ignore it.
